title: Beyond the blue horizon
subtitle: Ancient voyagers who settled the far-flung islands of the Pacific Ocean
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.

bodyParagraphs.text: Ancient voyagers who settled the far-flung islands of the Pacific Ocean

An important archaeological discovery on the island of Éfaté in the Pacific archipelago of Vanuatu has revealed traces of an ancient seafaring people, the distant ancestors of today’s Polynesians. The site came to light only by chance. An agricultural worker, digging in the grounds of a derelict plantation, scraped open a grave – the first of dozens in a burial ground some 3,000 years old. It is the oldest cemetery ever found in the Pacific islands, and it harbors the remains of an ancient people archaeologists call the Lapita.

They were daring blue-water adventurers who used basic canoes to rove across the ocean. But they were not just explorers. They were also pioneers who carried with them everything they would need to build new lives – their livestock, taro seedlings and stone tools. Within the span of several centuries, the Lapita stretched the boundaries of their world from the jungle-clad volcanoes of Papua New Guinea to the loneliest coral outliers of Tonga.

The Lapita left precious few clues about themselves, but Éfaté expands the volume of data available to researchers dramatically. The remains of 62 individuals have been uncovered so far, and archaeologists were also thrilled to find six complete Lapita pots. Other items included a Lapita burial urn with modeled birds arranged on the rim as though peering down at the human remains sealed inside. ‘It’s an important discovery,’ says Matthew Spriggs, professor of archaeology at the Australian National University and head of the international team digging up the site, ‘for it conclusively identifies the remains as Lapita.’

DNA teased from these human remains may help answer one of the most puzzling questions in Pacific anthropology: did all Pacific islanders spring from one source or many? Was there only one outward migration from a single point in Asia, or several from different points? ‘This represents the best opportunity we’ve had yet,’ says Spriggs, ‘to find out who the Lapita actually were, where they came from, and who their closest descendants are today.’

There is one stubborn question for which archaeology has yet to provide any answers: how did the Lapita accomplish the ancient equivalent of a moon landing, many times over? No-one has found one of their canoes or any rigging, which could reveal how the canoes were sailed. Nor do the oral histories and traditions of later Polynesians offer any insights, for they turn into myths long before they reach as far back in time as the Lapita.

‘All we can say for certain is that the Lapita had canoes that were capable of ocean voyages, and they had the ability to sail them,’ says Geoff Irwin, a professor of archaeology at the University of Auckland. Those sailing skills, he says, were developed and passed down over thousands of years by earlier mariners who worked their way through the archipelagoes of the western Pacific, making short crossings to nearby islands. The real adventure didn’t begin, however, until their Lapita descendants sailed out of sight of land, with empty horizons on every side. This must have been as difficult for them as landing on the moon is for us today. Certainly it distinguished them from their ancestors, but what gave them the courage to launch out on such risky voyages?

The Lapita’s thrust into the Pacific was eastward, against the prevailing trade winds, Irwin notes. Those nagging headwinds, he argues, may have been the key to their success. ‘They could sail out for days into the unknown and assess the area, secure in the knowledge that if they didn’t find anything, they could turn about and catch a swift ride back on the trade winds. This is what would have made the whole thing work.’ Once out there, skilled seafarers would have detected abundant leads to follow to land: seabirds, coconuts and twigs carried out to sea by the tides, and the afternoon pile-up of clouds on the horizon which often indicates an island in the distance.

For returning explorers, successful or not, the geography of their own archipelagoes would have provided a safety net. Without this to go by, overshooting their home ports, getting lost and sailing off into eternity would have been all too easy. Vanuatu, for example, stretches more than 500 miles in a northwest-southeast trend, its scores of intervisible islands forming a backstop for mariners riding the trade winds home.

All this presupposes one essential detail, says Atholl Anderson, professor of prehistory at the Australian National University: the Lapita had mastered the advanced art of sailing against the wind. ‘And there’s no proof they could do any such thing,’ Anderson says. ‘There has been this assumption they did, and people have built canoes to re-create those early voyages based on that assumption. But nobody has any idea what their canoes looked like or how they were rigged.’

Rather than give all the credit to human skill, Anderson invokes the winds of chance. El Niño, the same climate disruption that affects the Pacific today, may have helped scatter the Lapita, Anderson suggests. He points out that climate data obtained from slow-growing corals around the Pacific indicate a series of unusually frequent El Niños around the time of the Lapita expansion. By reversing the regular east-to-west flow of the trade winds for weeks at a time, these ‘super El Niños’ might have taken the Lapita on long unplanned voyages.

However they did it, the Lapita spread themselves a third of the way across the Pacific, then called it quits for reasons known only to them. Ahead lay the vast emptiness of the central Pacific and perhaps they were too thinly stretched to venture farther. They probably never numbered more than a few thousand in total, and in their rapid migration eastward they encountered hundreds of islands – more than 300 in Fiji alone.

questionGroups.summaryText:
A 3,000-year-old burial ground of a seafaring people called the Lapita has been found on an abandoned 27 ______ on the Pacific island of Éfaté. The cemetery, which is a significant 28 ______, was uncovered accidentally by an agricultural worker.

The burial ground increases the amount of information about the Lapita available to scientists. Spriggs believes the 30 ______ which was found at the site is very important since it confirms that the 31 ______ found inside are Lapita.

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.label: D

options.translation: 骨骼

options.label: E

options.translation: 数据

options.label: F

options.translation: 考古发现

options.label: G

options.label: H

questions.prompt: on an abandoned ______ on the Pacific island of Éfaté
questions.translation: 位于埃法特岛一处废弃的______上
questions.evidence: in the grounds of a derelict plantation
questions.locationLogic: abandoned paraphrases derelict; the required place is plantation.

distractors.C: The site is on land, not in a harbour.
distractors.F: This describes the cemetery’s significance, not its location.
distractors.J: No maps were found at the site.

questions.prompt: The cemetery, which is a significant ______, was uncovered accidentally
questions.translation: 这座墓地是一项重要的______，却是偶然发现的
questions.evidence: ‘It’s an important discovery,’ says Matthew Spriggs
questions.locationLogic: significant corresponds to important; cemetery discovery corresponds to archaeological discovery.

distractors.A: Proof is what the find provides, not what the cemetery itself is called.
distractors.E: Data is increased by the site but is not the type of find.
distractors.H: Source does not fit the noun description of the cemetery.

questions.evidence: their livestock, taro seedlings and stone tools
questions.locationLogic: livestock is the category animals; tools is already supplied after the blank.

distractors.D: Bones were found in the cemetery, not carried to build new lives.
distractors.G: The burial urn was a site find, not voyage equipment.

questions.prompt: Spriggs believes the ______ which was found at the site is very important
questions.translation: 斯普里格斯认为遗址中发现的______非常重要
questions.evidence: a Lapita burial urn with modeled birds arranged on the rim
questions.locationLogic: The singular object containing remains is the burial urn.

distractors.D: bones is plural and belongs in blank 31.
distractors.F: The general discovery is not the singular object found inside/containing remains.
distractors.A: Proof is an abstract result, not the excavated object.

questions.prompt: it confirms that the ______ found inside are Lapita
questions.translation: 它证实在里面发现的______属于拉皮塔人
questions.evidence: the human remains sealed inside ... it conclusively identifies the remains as Lapita
questions.locationLogic: human remains inside the urn are represented by bones; plural grammar matches are.

distractors.I: animals were carried by voyagers, not sealed inside this urn.
distractors.E: data is not a physical plural item inside the urn.
distractors.A: proof is uncountable and cannot take are.

instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.
Write the correct letter in boxes 32–35 on your answer sheet.

questions.prompt: According to the writer, there are difficulties explaining how the Lapita accomplished their journeys because
questions.translation: 作者认为，解释拉皮塔人如何完成航行存在困难，是因为

options.label: A
options.text: the canoes that have been discovered offer relatively few clues.
options.translation: 已发现的独木舟提供的线索相对很少。

options.label: B
options.text: archaeologists have shown limited interest in this area of research.
options.translation: 考古学家对这一研究领域兴趣有限。

options.label: C
options.text: little information relating to this period can be relied upon for accuracy.
options.translation: 与这一时期有关、可以信赖其准确性的信息很少。

options.label: D
options.text: technological advances have altered the way such achievements are viewed.
options.translation: 技术进步改变了人们看待这类成就的方式。

questions.evidence: No-one has found one of their canoes or any rigging ... oral histories and traditions ... turn into myths
questions.locationLogic: No physical craft survives and later accounts become myths, so reliable period evidence is scarce.

distractors.A: The passage says no canoe has been found, not that discovered canoes provide few clues.
distractors.B: Researchers are interested; lack of evidence is the problem.
distractors.D: No changed evaluation caused by technology is discussed.

questions.prompt: According to the sixth paragraph, what was extraordinary about the Lapita?
questions.translation: 根据第六段，拉皮塔人非同寻常之处是什么？

options.label: A
options.text: They sailed beyond the point where land was visible.
options.translation: 他们航行到了看不见陆地的地方。

options.label: B
options.text: Their cultural heritage discouraged the expression of fear.
options.translation: 他们的文化传统不鼓励表达恐惧。

options.label: C
options.text: They were able to build canoes that withstood ocean voyages.
options.translation: 他们能建造经得住远洋航行的独木舟。

options.label: D
options.text: Their navigational skills were passed on from one generation to the next.
options.translation: 他们的航海技能代代相传。

questions.evidence: their Lapita descendants sailed out of sight of land, with empty horizons on every side ... it distinguished them from their ancestors
questions.locationLogic: The distinguishing act was leaving all visible land behind.

distractors.B: Fear expression and cultural rules are not mentioned.
distractors.C: Ocean-capable canoes and sailing ability are all that is certain, not the specific distinguishing feat.
distractors.D: Skills were passed down by earlier mariners; inheritance itself did not distinguish the Lapita.

questions.prompt: What does ‘This’ refer to in the seventh paragraph?

options.label: A
options.text: the Lapita’s seafaring talent
options.translation: 拉皮塔人的航海才能

options.label: B
options.text: the Lapita’s ability to detect signs of land
options.translation: 拉皮塔人发现陆地迹象的能力

options.label: C
options.text: the Lapita’s extensive knowledge of the region
options.translation: 拉皮塔人对该地区的广博知识

options.label: D
options.text: the Lapita’s belief they would be able to return home
options.translation: 拉皮塔人相信自己能够返航

questions.evidence: secure in the knowledge that if they didn’t find anything, they could turn about and catch a swift ride back ... This is what would have made the whole thing work
questions.locationLogic: This refers to confidence that the trade winds would carry them home.

distractors.A: General skill is broader than the immediately preceding idea.
distractors.B: Detecting land signs is discussed only after This.
distractors.C: No extensive regional knowledge is stated.

questions.prompt: According to the eighth paragraph, how was the geography of the region significant?
questions.translation: 根据第八段，该地区的地理环境有何重要作用？

options.label: A
options.text: It played an important role in Lapita culture.
options.translation: 它在拉皮塔文化中发挥重要作用。

options.label: B
options.text: It meant there were relatively few storms at sea.
options.translation: 这意味着海上风暴相对较少。

options.label: C
options.text: It provided a navigational aid for the Lapita.
options.translation: 它为拉皮塔人提供了航海辅助。

options.label: D
options.text: It made a large number of islands habitable.
options.translation: 它使许多岛屿适宜居住。

questions.evidence: the geography of their own archipelagoes would have provided a safety net ... intervisible islands forming a backstop for mariners riding the trade winds home
questions.locationLogic: The chain of visible islands helped navigators avoid missing home ports.

distractors.B: No claim is made about fewer storms.
distractors.D: The paragraph concerns finding the route home, not habitability.

instructions: Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer in Reading Passage 3?
In boxes 36–40 on your answer sheet, write
YES if the statement agrees with the views of the writer
NO if the statement contradicts the views of the writer
NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this

questions.prompt: It is now clear that the Lapita could sail into a prevailing wind.
questions.translation: 如今已经明确，拉皮塔人能够逆着盛行风航行。
questions.evidence: the Lapita had mastered the advanced art of sailing against the wind. ‘And there’s no proof they could do any such thing,’
questions.locationLogic: The claim that it is clear directly contradicts the stated absence of proof.

distractors.YES: The ability is a presupposition, not an established fact.
distractors.NOT GIVEN: The writer explicitly reports that there is no proof.

questions.prompt: Extreme climate conditions may have played a role in Lapita migration.
questions.translation: 极端气候条件可能在拉皮塔人的迁徙中发挥了作用。
questions.evidence: unusually frequent El Niños ... these ‘super El Niños’ might have taken the Lapita on long unplanned voyages
questions.locationLogic: Super El Niños are extreme climate events proposed as a possible migration driver.

distractors.NO: The passage proposes, rather than rejects, the climate explanation.
distractors.NOT GIVEN: The possible role is explicitly stated.

questions.prompt: The Lapita learnt to predict the duration of El Niños.
questions.translation: 拉皮塔人学会了预测厄尔尼诺现象持续的时间。
questions.evidence: climate data ... indicate a series of unusually frequent El Niños ... reversing ... winds for weeks at a time
questions.locationLogic: The text discusses modern climate evidence and event duration, not Lapita prediction skills.

distractors.YES: No learning or prediction is reported.
distractors.NO: The writer does not say they were unable to predict it.

questions.prompt: It remains unclear why the Lapita halted their expansion across the Pacific.
questions.translation: 拉皮塔人为何停止向太平洋扩张，至今仍不清楚。
questions.evidence: then called it quits for reasons known only to them
questions.locationLogic: Reasons known only to the Lapita are unavailable to present observers, so the cause remains unclear.

distractors.NO: The next sentence offers only a possibility, not a settled explanation.

questions.prompt: It is likely that the majority of Lapita settled on Fiji.
questions.translation: 大多数拉皮塔人很可能定居在斐济。
questions.evidence: they encountered hundreds of islands – more than 300 in Fiji alone
questions.locationLogic: The number of islands encountered in Fiji gives no population distribution or majority settlement claim.

distractors.YES: Many islands in Fiji does not mean most people settled there.
distractors.NO: The passage does not state that a majority settled elsewhere.
